analysis.one_liner: Shuts down the Export-Import Bank, the government agency that subsidizes exports.
analysis.headline: The bill to shut down the Export-Import Bank was referred to the House Financial Services Committee and never received a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have abolished the Export-Import Bank, a government agency that finances and insures exports by American companies, mostly large ones like aircraft makers. It would have stopped the Bank from taking new applications almost immediately and wound down its existing obligations over three years under the Treasury Department. The bill never received a vote; it sat in the Financial Services Committee until the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: If enacted, taxpayers would stop backing a federal agency that guarantees private banks' export loans, and small domestic businesses that compete with heavily subsidized exporters would face a fairer field. Its findings argue most Ex-Im financing benefits large multinationals rather than small businesses.

how_it_helps.text: It would abolish the Export-Import Bank three years after enactment, with a Treasury-managed wind-down of outstanding obligations [S2, S3].
It would stop the Bank from accepting new applications for loans, insurance, or guarantees within 30 days of enactment, ending the flow of new export subsidies [S3].

Its stated rationale is that export subsidies advantage specific large businesses at the expense of domestic competitors and the public, and that most of the Bank's financing subsidizes large multinational corporations rather than small businesses [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Large exporters that rely on Ex-Im loan guarantees and insurance for big foreign sales — especially aerospace and heavy equipment firms — and the banks that originate the underlying loans, would lose a federal backstop for that credit.

drawbacks.text: The bill's own findings acknowledge the counterargument it must answer: most Ex-Im financing backs exports by large multinational corporations, and critics of elimination warned foreign governments' export-credit agencies would fill the gap, potentially costing American exporters — and their workers — sales abroad [S3].
The bill would have ended new loan, insurance, and guarantee applications almost immediately, which could have disrupted financing for pending export deals during the wind-down period [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main benefit is ending a federal export subsidy that the bill argues favors large multinationals and shifts risk to taxpayers; the main costs are that exporters could lose sales to foreign competitors backed by their own export-credit agencies, and that some exporter jobs might suffer — the strongest good-faith objection to ending the Bank. The bill did not become law, so neither cost nor benefit was realized.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Financial Services Committee, which never acted on it, so it died there.

narrative.text: Rep. Justin Amash introduced the Export-Import Bank Termination Act on March 25, 2015 [S1, S5].
The House referred it to the Committee on Financial Services the same day; no further action appears in the record for the rest of the 114th Congress [S5].
It drew 9 Republican cosponsors and no Democratic support [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The exporters and banks that rely on Export-Import Bank financing, which kept their federal backing; the Bank itself also survived, though its charter lapsed briefly in mid-2015 before Congress later reauthorized it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Export-Im Bank's corporate clients and partner banks

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no action; the bill never reached the House floor.

against.name: Boeing and other major Ex-Im clients
against.role: Large exporters dependent on Ex-Im financing
against.what_they_did: Publicly campaigned to preserve the Export-Import Bank during the 2015 reauthorization fight.

sides.party_line_note: All 9 cosponsors were Republicans; no Democrat supported the bill [S4].

industries.industry: Large exporters (aircraft makers, heavy equipment and energy firms)
industries.note: These firms are the largest users of Ex-Im loan guarantees and insurance for foreign sales. Losing the Bank would have removed a subsidy that keeps their export deals financed.
Private banks profit from Ex-Im guarantees and insurance on the trade credit they extend. The bill's findings state these institutions also profit from the export subsidies [S3].

industries.industry: Small domestic businesses that compete against subsidized exporters
industries.note: The bill argues export subsidies favor specific industries at the expense of domestic competition, so ending them would level the field for firms that receive no such support [S3].
The bill argues the Bank's true expected return is far lower than official estimates and that taxpayers bear the downside risk of the guaranteed loans, as with prior federal credit programs [S3].
